items.title: Your Brain on Books
items.description: What’s happening in your brain and body while you’re lost in a great book? Is reading print fundamentally different from reading on a screen? And how can you get the most restorative benefits from your reading habits? We’re covering these questions and much more in Big Think’s upcoming members-only event, Your Brain on Books. items.title: The philosophy of liberalism and how it has transformed our institutions
items.description:
Jonathan Rauch, author and senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, dives into the philosophy of liberalism, how it has created and transformed our institutions, and the state of truth in a world rife with misinformation.  
 This video  The philosophy of liberalism and how it has transformed our institutions  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: The secret to reading more classics? Don’t treat them like homework.
items.description:
I have never read  Crime and Punishment  (1867). I’ve been meaning to for years and thought my moment had come  last winter , after a weekend spent researching the best translation for a Dostoevsky newbie. Then life happened, as it does, and the moment skittered on by. I set my brand-new copy on the shelf, and it has been sitting there ever since, spine uncracked, its pristine pages a testament to my lapse.

items.description:
Map fans and book lovers: Now that’s a Venn diagram with a big overlap. Why? “Because, like books, maps contain  stories . items.title: The gap between knowing better and doing better, and how to close it
items.description:
Most of us can recite the benefits of exercise, gratitude, and patience while doing none of it. Tal Ben-Shahar calls this the Knowing-Doing gap, and our typical interventions, like retreats and month-long overhauls, keep it open. 
 
 This video  The gap between knowing better and doing better, and how to close it  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: Scratching the surface: A field guide to 100 essential novels
items.description:
If you’re not a member, then probably someone you know or love is: that shrinking, but still substantial guild of book-balancers who build towers of paperbacks on their nightstands.  
 Few things are as enjoyable as finishing a good book, except perhaps starting a new one, and because the latter is easier than the former, the job is never done. Hence that precipitously perched tower of books.

items.title: 25 years later, “Donnie Darko” is finally getting a sequel
items.description:
By all accounts,  Donnie Darko  shouldn’t exist.  
 The film, which turns 25 years old this year, ran into numerous obstacles both before and during its storied production. items.title: Ask Ethan: If intelligent alien life exists, will we make contact?
items.description: For countless generations, humanity has gazed at the stars, planets, and great canopy of the Milky Way in the night sky, wondering who else or what else may be out there. items.title: “Donnie Darko” offers a time travel lesson you won’t find elsewhere
items.description: In film, there are many ways to tell a story that involves time travel. Some movies, such as the  Terminator  franchise, simply include the phenomenon as a plot device, reckoning that the technical explanation is unimportant to the plot. Other times, as in  Groundhog Day , characters get stuck in a time loop, only breaking out of it once a moral lesson is learned.
